Haiden | location = 1371 Maki, Ōita City, Ōita Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E|region:JP-44|display=inline,title}} | deity = Spirits of the war dead and public servants from Ōita Prefecture | type = Formerly Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Shrine; {{ill|Betsu Hyōsha|ja|別表神社|12=draft}} | established = October 18, 1875 (Meiji 8)[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/history/ History and Origin] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | festivals = {{ubl|April 9 (Spring Grand festival)|October 9 (Autumn Grand festival)}} | map = {{location map|Japan Oita|label=Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}}} }} {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Ōita Gokoku Shrine|ja|大分縣護國神社}} (大分縣護國神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Ōita City|ja|大分市|12=draft}}, Ōita Prefecture, [[Japan]]. It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|12=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| Torii File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|12=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 Haiden | location = 1371 Maki, Ōita City, Ōita Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E|region:JP-44|display=inline,title}} | deity = Spirits of the war dead and public servants from Ōita Prefecture | type = Formerly Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Shrine; {{ill|Betsu Hyōsha|ja|別表神社|12=draft}} | established = October 18, 1875 (Meiji 8)[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/history/ History and Origin] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | festivals = {{ubl|April 9 (Spring Grand festival)|October 9 (Autumn Grand festival)}} | map = {{location map|Japan Oita|label=Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}}} }} {{Interlanguage link|12=draft|Ōita Gokoku Shrine|ja|大分縣護國神社}} (大分縣護國神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Ōita City|ja|大分市|12=draft}}, Ōita Prefecture, [[Japan]]. It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|12=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| Torii File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|12=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft|12=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|12=draft|12=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft|12=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| Torii File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft|12=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|12=draft|12=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft|12=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| Torii File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * Haiden | location = 1371 Maki, Ōita City, Ōita Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E|region:JP-44|display=inline,title}} | deity = Spirits of the war dead and public servants from Ōita Prefecture | type = Formerly Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Shrine; {{ill|Betsu Hyōsha|ja|別表神社|12=draft|12=draft}} | established = October 18, 1875 (Meiji 8)[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/history/ History and Origin] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | festivals = {{ubl|April 9 (Spring Grand festival)|October 9 (Autumn Grand festival)}} | map = {{location map|Japan Oita|label=Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}}} }} {{ill|Ōita Gokoku Shrine|ja|大分縣護國神社}} (大分縣護國神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|12=draft|12=draft}} located in {{ill|Ōita City|ja|大分市|12=draft|12=draft}}, Ōita Prefecture, [[Japan]]. It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|12=draft|12=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|12=draft|12=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|12=draft|12=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| Torii File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the Haiden | location = 1371 Maki, Ōita City, Ōita Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E|region:JP-44|display=inline,title}} | deity = Spirits of the war dead and public servants from Ōita Prefecture | type = Formerly Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Shrine; {{ill|Betsu Hyōsha|ja|別表神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} | established = October 18, 1875 (Meiji 8)[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/history/ History and Origin] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | festivals = {{ubl|April 9 (Spring Grand festival)|October 9 (Autumn Grand festival)}} | map = {{location map|Japan Oita|label=Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}}} }} {{ill|Ōita Gokoku Shrine|ja|大分縣護國神社}} (大分縣護國神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in {{ill|Ōita City|ja|大分市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Ōita Prefecture, [[Japan]]. It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| Torii File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine temple]] and [[:en:Wen Wu temple|Wen Wu temple]] * [[National Revolutionary Martyrs' Shrine]] * [[Eternal Spring Shrine]] * [[:en:Chinese Cultural Renaissance|Chinese Cultural Renaissance]] * {{神社 |名称 = 大分縣護國神社 |画像 = [[File:Oita gokoku jinja1.jpg|280px]]
拝殿 |所在地 = [[大分県]][[大分市]]大字牧1371[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 大分県護國神社] 一般社団法人 大分市観光協会 |位置 = {{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E|region:JP-44_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} |祭神 = 大分県縁故の英霊 |社格 = 旧内務大臣指定[[護国神社]]・[[別表神社]] |創建 = [[明治]]8年（[[1875年]]）[[10月18日]][http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/history/ 由緒・歴史] 大分縣護國神社 |本殿 = [[流造]] |別名 = |札所等 = |例祭 = 4月9日・10月9日[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html 恒例行事] 大分縣護國神社 |神事 = |地図 = {{Location map|Japan Oita|label=大分縣
護國神社|coordinates= {{coord2|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}}} }} '''大分縣護國神社'''（おおいたけんごこくじんじゃ）は、[[大分県]][[大分市]]にある[[神社]]（[[護国神社]]）である。 == 概要 == 大分市中央部の小山、[[松栄山]]の中腹に社地を構える。 境内には[[ウメ#主な品種|豊後梅]]を中心とする約200本の[[ウメ|梅]]と約500本の[[サクラ|桜]]があり、梅と桜の名所として知られる。3月の第1日曜日には梅花祭が開かれる。 大分市が[[2006年]]（平成18年）に実施した「私が選ぶおおいた100景」のアンケートでは、護國神社からの[[大分臨海工業地帯]]の眺望が3位に入っている[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “私が選ぶおおいた100景”市民アンケート結果] 大分市。 == 祭神 == 大分県縁故の戦没者約4万4千柱を主[[祭神]]とし、[[殉職]][[日本の警察官|警察官]]・[[自衛官]]を[[相殿]]に祀る。 == 沿革 == 松栄山は古くから景勝の地として知られていた。[[1799年]]（[[寛政]]11年）には、[[伏見城の戦い]]で没した[[大給松平家]]の祖先[[松平近正]]の二百[[年忌]]にあたることから、当時の[[府内藩]]主[[松平近儔]]が[[府内城]]東北の山里曲輪にあった近正の祠を松栄山に移し、近正大明神として祀った。「松栄」の名も、松平家が栄えることを願って付けられたものとされる。近正大明神の霊宮は[[1869年]]（[[明治]]2年）に大分市中心部の堀川（現在の[[都町 (大分市)|都町]]付近）に遷座して松栄神社と名付けられた後、[[1900年]]（明治33年）に旧地である[[荷揚町]]の府内城山里曲輪跡に遷している渡辺克己「{{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf 大分今昔 第二十七章 萩原かいわい]}}」 大分合同新聞社、2008年2月15日。 大分縣護國神社は、大分県初代[[県令]][[森下景端]]が、[[1874年]]（明治7年）に起きた[[佐賀の乱]]の[[戦死]]者14柱、[[台湾出兵]]での[[戦病死]]者3柱に、[[明治維新]]の[[勤王]]の[[志士]]など5柱を合わせて祀り、慰霊顕彰を行うために、[[1875年]]（明治8年）[[10月18日]]に、霊宮が遷座した後の松栄山山頂に[[招魂社]]を創建したのに始まる。 [[1939年]]（[[昭和]]14年）4月に、招魂社の制度改正により大分縣護國神社に改称し、[[内務大臣 (日本)|内務大臣]]指定護国神社となった。かつての社殿は境内北側の現在展望台となっている付近にあったが、[[1943年]]（昭和18年）[[10月28日]]に現在地に遷座した。 [[1945年]]（昭和20年）の[[第二次世界大戦|第二次大戦]]敗戦以降は「豊霊宮」と称していたが、日本の主権回復後の[[1952年]]（昭和27年）9月に元の大分縣護國神社に復した。 [[1966年]]（昭和41年）[[10月22日]]、[[昭和天皇]]、[[香淳皇后]]が[[第21回国民体育大会]]に合わせて県内を行幸啓。護国神社が訪問先の一つとなった{{Cite book |和書 |author=原武史 |title=昭和天皇御召列車全記録 |publisher=新潮社 |year=2016-09-30 |page=129 |isbn=978-4-10-320523-4}}。 [[2024年]]（令和6年）には同年5月26日に閉館式が行われた大分予科練資料館にあった収蔵品の寄託を受けることになった{{Cite web|和書|date=2024-05-26 |url=https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2024/05/26/JDC2024052602161 |title=「大分予科練資料館」36年の歴史に幕　現地で閉館式、収蔵品移設へ寄付募る |publisher=大分合同新聞 |accessdate=2024-05-27}}。 == 祭祀 == * 歳旦祭 - [[1月1日]] * [[紀元節|紀元祭]] - [[2月11日]] * 春季例大祭 - [[4月9日]] * みたま祭 - [[8月13日]]-[[8月15日]] * 秋期例大祭 - [[10月9日]] * [[天長祭]] - [[12月23日]] == 境内 == * 慰霊碑 - 大分県関係戦没者の慰霊塔を中にして、右に元[[歩兵第47連隊|歩兵第47聯隊]]戦没者慰霊の「軍旗の碑」、左に大分県出身[[海軍飛行予科練習生|予科練]]戦没者慰霊の「鎮魂の碑」が建っている[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html 境内のご案内] 大分縣護國神社。 * 言霊記念館 - 展示館。[[特別攻撃隊|特攻隊員]]が残した遺書や手紙を掲示するほか、写真やビデオ上映も行われている。 * 満蒙開拓義勇軍碑 - [[1938年]]（昭和13年）、満蒙（[[満州]]・[[内蒙古]]）へ開拓のため組織され派遣された[[満蒙開拓青少年義勇軍]]の記念碑。銃と鍬を手に持つ隊員の像、[[レリーフ]]がある。 * 西南の役軍人墓地 - [[1877年]]（明治10年）の[[西南戦争|西南の役]]に際し戦死した陸軍軍人214柱の墓地。展望台、豊後梅の梅林の奥にある。[[鹿児島県|鹿児島]]、[[山口県|山口]]など、[[薩長]]出身者が多い。西南の役の戦死者墓地はこの軍人墓地と次項の警察官墓地の2つに分かれている。 * 西南の役警察官墓地 - 西南の役に際し戦死した103柱の[[警視隊]]墓地。表参道百段の脇にある。[[青森県|青森]]、[[秋田県|秋田]]、[[福島県|福島]]をはじめとする[[東北地方|東北]]出身の[[士族]]が多い。戊辰戦争で薩長と戦った元[[会津藩]]家老[[佐川官兵衛]]も[[熊本県]][[阿蘇郡]]で戦死し、この墓地に警察官として埋葬されている田中悟「[https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1050294045371617152 死者の記憶と「非業さ」：白虎隊・佐川官兵衛をめぐって]」 政治経済史学 490号、pp.1-26、2007年6月、政治経済史学会。 * 展望台 * 招魂齋庭 - 創建当時の招魂社の跡地。 * 大絵馬 - 縦3m、横5mの絵馬で、九州最大とされる。毎年の干支が描かれ、年末から3月末まで設置される。 * 大はま矢 - 高さ18.8m、重さ1.8tで日本一の大きさとされる。年末から3月末まで設置される[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 大きな願いかないそう 日本一の破魔矢と熊手 県護国神社] 大分合同新聞、2016年12月4日。 * 大熊手 - 高さ12m、重さ5.1tで日本一の大きさとされる。 * [[特攻勇士の像]] - [[2014年]]（平成26年）9月建立[http://www.tokkotai.or.jp/statues 特攻像建立状況] 公益財団法人特攻隊戦没者慰霊顕彰会。 == ギャラリー == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| 大はまやと巨大熊手 File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| 鳥居 File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 03.jpg| 大分縣護國神社の桜 == 交通 == * 鉄道：[[九州旅客鉄道|JR九州]][[日豊本線]][[高城駅]]からタクシーで約5分、徒歩で約20分[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html アクセス] 大分縣護國神社。 * バス：JR九州[[大分駅]]から、[[大分バス]]で城東中学校停留所下車、徒歩17分。 * 自動車：[[大分自動車道|大分道]]・[[東九州自動車道|東九州道]][[大分米良インターチェンジ|米良IC]]から車で約20分。 == 脚注 == {{reflist|2}} == 外部リンク == * [http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/ 大分縣護國神社]（神社公式） {{神道 横}} {{神社 |名称 = 大分縣護國神社 |画像 = [[File:Oita gokoku jinja1.jpg|280px]]
拝殿 |所在地 = [[大分県]][[大分市]]大字牧1371[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 大分県護國神社] 一般社団法人 大分市観光協会 |位置 = {{ウィキ座標2段度分秒|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E|region:JP-44_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} |祭神 = 大分県縁故の英霊 |社格 = 旧内務大臣指定[[護国神社]]・[[別表神社]] |創建 = [[明治]]8年（[[1875年]]）[[10月18日]][http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/history/ 由緒・歴史] 大分縣護國神社 |本殿 = [[流造]] |別名 = |札所等 = |例祭 = 4月9日・10月9日[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html 恒例行事] 大分縣護國神社 |神事 = |地図 = {{Location map|Japan Oita|label=大分縣
護國神社|coordinates= {{coord2|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}}} }} '''大分縣護國神社'''（おおいたけんごこくじんじゃ）は、[[大分県]][[大分市]]にある[[神社]]（[[護国神社]]）である。 == 概要 == 大分市中央部の小山、[[松栄山]]の中腹に社地を構える。 境内には[[ウメ#主な品種|豊後梅]]を中心とする約200本の[[ウメ|梅]]と約500本の[[サクラ|桜]]があり、梅と桜の名所として知られる。3月の第1日曜日には梅花祭が開かれる。 大分市が[[2006年]]（平成18年）に実施した「私が選ぶおおいた100景」のアンケートでは、護國神社からの[[大分臨海工業地帯]]の眺望が3位に入っている[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “私が選ぶおおいた100景”市民アンケート結果] 大分市。 == 祭神 == 大分県縁故の戦没者約4万4千柱を主[[祭神]]とし、[[殉職]][[日本の警察官|警察官]]・[[自衛官]]を[[相殿]]に祀る。 == 沿革 == 松栄山は古くから景勝の地として知られていた。[[1799年]]（[[寛政]]11年）には、[[伏見城の戦い]]で没した[[大給松平家]]の祖先[[松平近正]]の二百[[年忌]]にあたることから、当時の[[府内藩]]主[[松平近儔]]が[[府内城]]東北の山里曲輪にあった近正の祠を松栄山に移し、近正大明神として祀った。「松栄」の名も、松平家が栄えることを願って付けられたものとされる。近正大明神の霊宮は[[1869年]]（[[明治]]2年）に大分市中心部の堀川（現在の[[都町 (大分市)|都町]]付近）に遷座して松栄神社と名付けられた後、[[1900年]]（明治33年）に旧地である[[荷揚町]]の府内城山里曲輪跡に遷している渡辺克己「{{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf 大分今昔 第二十七章 萩原かいわい]}}」 大分合同新聞社、2008年2月15日。 大分縣護國神社は、大分県初代[[県令]][[森下景端]]が、[[1874年]]（明治7年）に起きた[[佐賀の乱]]の[[戦死]]者14柱、[[台湾出兵]]での[[戦病死]]者3柱に、[[明治維新]]の[[勤王]]の[[志士]]など5柱を合わせて祀り、慰霊顕彰を行うために、[[1875年]]（明治8年）[[10月18日]]に、霊宮が遷座した後の松栄山山頂に[[招魂社]]を創建したのに始まる。 [[1939年]]（[[昭和]]14年）4月に、招魂社の制度改正により大分縣護國神社に改称し、[[内務大臣 (日本)|内務大臣]]指定護国神社となった。かつての社殿は境内北側の現在展望台となっている付近にあったが、[[1943年]]（昭和18年）[[10月28日]]に現在地に遷座した。 [[1945年]]（昭和20年）の[[第二次世界大戦|第二次大戦]]敗戦以降は「豊霊宮」と称していたが、日本の主権回復後の[[1952年]]（昭和27年）9月に元の大分縣護國神社に復した。 [[1966年]]（昭和41年）[[10月22日]]、[[昭和天皇]]、[[香淳皇后]]が[[第21回国民体育大会]]に合わせて県内を行幸啓。護国神社が訪問先の一つとなった{{Cite book |和書 |author=原武史 |title=昭和天皇御召列車全記録 |publisher=新潮社 |year=2016-09-30 |page=129 |isbn=978-4-10-320523-4}}。 [[2024年]]（令和6年）には同年5月26日に閉館式が行われた大分予科練資料館にあった収蔵品の寄託を受けることになった{{Cite web|和書|date=2024-05-26 |url=https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2024/05/26/JDC2024052602161 |title=「大分予科練資料館」36年の歴史に幕　現地で閉館式、収蔵品移設へ寄付募る |publisher=大分合同新聞 |accessdate=2024-05-27}}。 == 祭祀 == * 歳旦祭 - [[1月1日]] * [[紀元節|紀元祭]] - [[2月11日]] * 春季例大祭 - [[4月9日]] * みたま祭 - [[8月13日]]-[[8月15日]] * 秋期例大祭 - [[10月9日]] * [[天長祭]] - [[12月23日]] == 境内 == * 慰霊碑 - 大分県関係戦没者の慰霊塔を中にして、右に元[[歩兵第47連隊|歩兵第47聯隊]]戦没者慰霊の「軍旗の碑」、左に大分県出身[[海軍飛行予科練習生|予科練]]戦没者慰霊の「鎮魂の碑」が建っている[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html 境内のご案内] 大分縣護國神社。 * 言霊記念館 - 展示館。[[特別攻撃隊|特攻隊員]]が残した遺書や手紙を掲示するほか、写真やビデオ上映も行われている。 * 満蒙開拓義勇軍碑 - [[1938年]]（昭和13年）、満蒙（[[満州]]・[[内蒙古]]）へ開拓のため組織され派遣された[[満蒙開拓青少年義勇軍]]の記念碑。銃と鍬を手に持つ隊員の像、[[レリーフ]]がある。 * 西南の役軍人墓地 - [[1877年]]（明治10年）の[[西南戦争|西南の役]]に際し戦死した陸軍軍人214柱の墓地。展望台、豊後梅の梅林の奥にある。[[鹿児島県|鹿児島]]、[[山口県|山口]]など、[[薩長]]出身者が多い。西南の役の戦死者墓地はこの軍人墓地と次項の警察官墓地の2つに分かれている。 * 西南の役警察官墓地 - 西南の役に際し戦死した103柱の[[警視隊]]墓地。表参道百段の脇にある。[[青森県|青森]]、[[秋田県|秋田]]、[[福島県|福島]]をはじめとする[[東北地方|東北]]出身の[[士族]]が多い。戊辰戦争で薩長と戦った元[[会津藩]]家老[[佐川官兵衛]]も[[熊本県]][[阿蘇郡]]で戦死し、この墓地に警察官として埋葬されている田中悟「[https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1050294045371617152 死者の記憶と「非業さ」：白虎隊・佐川官兵衛をめぐって]」 政治経済史学 490号、pp.1-26、2007年6月、政治経済史学会。 * 展望台 * 招魂齋庭 - 創建当時の招魂社の跡地。 * 大絵馬 - 縦3m、横5mの絵馬で、九州最大とされる。毎年の干支が描かれ、年末から3月末まで設置される。 * 大はま矢 - 高さ18.8m、重さ1.8tで日本一の大きさとされる。年末から3月末まで設置される[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 大きな願いかないそう 日本一の破魔矢と熊手 県護国神社] 大分合同新聞、2016年12月4日。 * 大熊手 - 高さ12m、重さ5.1tで日本一の大きさとされる。 * [[特攻勇士の像]] - [[2014年]]（平成26年）9月建立[http://www.tokkotai.or.jp/statues 特攻像建立状況] 公益財団法人特攻隊戦没者慰霊顕彰会。 == ギャラリー == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| 大はまやと巨大熊手 File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| 鳥居 File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 03.jpg| 大分縣護國神社の桜 == 交通 == * 鉄道：[[九州旅客鉄道|JR九州]][[日豊本線]][[高城駅]]からタクシーで約5分、徒歩で約20分[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html アクセス] 大分縣護國神社。 * バス：JR九州[[大分駅]]から、[[大分バス]]で城東中学校停留所下車、徒歩17分。 * 自動車：[[大分自動車道|大分道]]・[[東九州自動車道|東九州道]][[大分米良インターチェンジ|米良IC]]から車で約20分。 == 脚注 == {{reflist|2}} == 外部リンク == * [http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/ 大分縣護國神社]（神社公式） {{神道 横}} Haiden | location = 1371 Maki, Ōita City, Ōita Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E|region:JP-44|display=inline,title}} | deity = Spirits of the war dead and public servants from Ōita Prefecture | type = Formerly Ministry of Interior-designated Gokoku Shrine; {{ill|Betsu Hyōsha|ja|別表神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} | established = October 18, 1875 (Meiji 8)[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/history/ History and Origin] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine | festivals = {{ubl|April 9 (Spring Grand festival)|October 9 (Autumn Grand festival)}} | map = {{location map|Japan Oita|label=Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|coord={{coord|33|14|06.5|N|131|38|31.3|E}}}} }} {{ill|Ōita Gokoku Shrine|ja|大分縣護國神社}} (大分縣護國神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in {{ill|Ōita City|ja|大分市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Ōita Prefecture, [[Japan]]. It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| Torii File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 {{ill|Satsuma Rebellion|ja|西南戦争|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the
