It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[:en:Ōita Station|Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[:en:Fuchū Domain|Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[JR Kyushu]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[:en:Ōita Station|Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[:en:Fuchū Domain|Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[:en:Ōita Station|Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[:en:Higashi Kyushu Expressway|Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[Matsudaira clan]], the [[:en:Fuchū Domain|Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[:en:Ōita Station|Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[:en:Higashi Kyushu Expressway|Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[:en:Matsudaira clan|Matsudaira clan]], the [[:en:Fuchū Domain|Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[:en:Ōita Station|Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[:en:Higashi Kyushu Expressway|Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[:en:Matsudaira clan|Matsudaira clan]], the [[:en:Fuchū Domain|Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[:en:Saga Rebellion|Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[:en:Ōita Station|Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[:en:Higashi Kyushu Expressway|Higashi Kyushu Expressway]]. == Gallery == File:Oita gokoku jinja2.jpg| Giant Hamaya and Kumade File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 01.jpg| Torii File:Oita Ken Gokoku Shrine 20200408 03.jpg| Sakura at Ōita It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[:en:Ume|Ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[:en:Matsudaira clan|Matsudaira clan]], the [[:en:Fuchū Domain|Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[:en:Saga Rebellion|Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[:en:Taiwan Expedition|Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]]'s [[Takajō Station]] on the [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[:en:Ōita Station|Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[:en:Higashi Kyushu Expressway|Higashi Kyushu It honors the spirits of war dead and public servants from the region. It is a [[Beppyo Shrine]], or a shrine that is particularly notable in a certain way with a significant history to it.{{Cite web |title=別表神社とは？御朱印めぐりに参考になる「別表神社一覧」とマップ {{!}} 開運戦隊ゴシュインジャー |url=https://jinja-gosyuin.com/beppyou/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=jinja-gosyuin.com}} It is a [[Gokoku Shrines|Gokoku Shrine]], or a shrine dedicated to war dead.{{Efn|Is this [[WP:BLUE]] considering that the shrine is literally named as such?}} Such shrines were made to serve to enshrine the war dead, and they were all considered "branches" of [[Yasukuni Shrine]]. They were renamed from [[Shōkonsha|Shokonsha]] in 1939.{{Cite journal |last=TAKAYAMA |first=K. PETER |date=1990 |title=Enshrinement and Persistency of Japanese Religion |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23917081 |journal=Journal of Church and State |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=527–547 |issn=0021-969X}} It was founded in 1875{{Cite web |last=bebeppu |date=2020-03-24 |title=Oita ken Gokoku shrine |url=https://bebeppu.com/en/gokoku-shrine/ |access-date=2023-10-22 |website=ビーベップ |language=en-US}} An old WWII flag taken by an American soldier was returned to it in 2022.{{Cite web |title=Navy vet’s daughter returns Japanese flag taken as war trophy from Battle of Okinawa |url=https://www.stripes.com/theaters/asia_pacific/2022-02-03/japanese-flag-return-battle-of-okinawa-us-navy-world-war-ii-4571775.html |access-date=2023-10-25 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}} A giant arrow was made at it.{{Cite news |date=2021-12-06 |title=Giant good-luck arrow, rake devoted to shrine in west Japan |language=en |work=Mainichi Daily News |url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20211206/p2a/00m/0na/030000c |access-date=2023-10-25}} == Overview == The shrine is situated halfway up [[Shōeizan]] (松栄山), a hill known for its scenic beauty.[https://www.oishiimati-oita.jp/spots/detail/CPID:44139 Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita City Tourism Association The precincts feature approximately 200 [[:en:Ume|Ume]] (plum) trees, mainly of the [[Bungo plum]] variety, and 500 [[:en:Sakura|Sakura]] (cherry blossom) trees, making it a popular spot for flower viewing. A Plum Blossom festival is held annually on the first Sunday of March. The view of the Ōita Coastal Industrial Zone from the shrine Ranked third in the "100 Best Views of Ōita" poll conducted by Ōita City in 2006.[http://www.city.oita.oita.jp/www/contents/1153979406476/index.html “100 Best Views of Ōita” Citizen Poll Results] Ōita City == Enshrined Deities == The shrine enshrines approximately 44,000 spirits of war dead and public servants, including police officers and members of the Self-Defense Forces. [[every:Oita Gokoku Shrine]] == History == Shōeizan has been a place of scenic beauty since ancient times. In 1799 (Kansei 11), the 200th anniversary of the death of [[Matsudaira Chikamasa]], ancestor of the [[:en:Matsudaira clan|Matsudaira clan]], the [[:en:Fuchū Domain|Fuchū Domain]] lord [[Matsudaira Chikamoto]] moved Chikamasa's shrine to Shōeizan and named it "Shōeizan Shrine" in hopes of the Matsudaira clan's prosperity.Watanabe Katsumi, {{PDFlink|[http://www.nan-nan.jp/lib/oita027a1.pdf Ōita Past and Present Chapter 27: Around Hagiwara]}} The foundation of Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine dates back to 1875 (Meiji 8), when the first governor of Ōita, [[Morishita Kagehira]], established a {{ill|Shōkonsha|ja|招魂社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkonsha|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} to honor 14 soldiers who died in the [[:en:Saga Rebellion|Saga Rebellion]], three who succumbed during the [[:en:Taiwan Expedition|Taiwan Expedition]], and five loyalists of the Meiji Restoration. In 1939 (Shōwa 14), the shrine was renamed Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine under the revised Shōkonsha system and was designated as a Gokoku Shrine by the Ministry of Interior. The shrine was relocated to its current location in 1943. After Japan's defeat in [[World War II]], the shrine was renamed "Toyorei Shrine." It reverted to Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine in 1952 following the restoration of Japanese sovereignty. == festivals and Rituals == * '''New Year's festival''': January 1 * '''Kigensetsu (National Foundation Day)''': February 11 * '''Spring Grand festival''': April 9 * '''Mitama festival''': August 13–15 * '''Autumn Grand festival''': October 9 * '''Tenchō festival''': December 23[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/annual_event/index.html annual Events] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine == Grounds == * '''Memorial Monuments''': Includes towers dedicated to war victims from Ōita Prefecture, the 47th Infantry Regiment, and naval aviation cadets. * '''Kotodama Memorial Hall''': Displays farewell letters and writings of {{ill|Japanese Special Attack Units|ja|特攻隊|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Special Attack Units|qq=}}.[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/guide/index.html Grounds Guide] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''Manchurian Youth Volunteer Corps Monument''': Commemorates youth sent to Manchuria for settlement. * '''Graves of Satsuma Rebellion Soldiers and Police Officers''': Dedicated to those who died during the 1877 [[:en:Satsuma Rebellion|Satsuma Rebellion]]. * '''Large Ema (Votive Tablet)''': The largest in Kyushu, measuring 3m by 5m. * '''Giant Hamaya (Arrow)''': Standing 18.8m tall and weighing 1.8 tons, it is the largest in Japan.[https://www.oita-press.co.jp/1010000000/2016/12/04/JD0055257100 Japan’s Largest Hamaya and Kumade at Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine] Ōita Press * '''Giant Kumade (Rake)''': 12m tall and 5.1 tons. == Access == * '''By Train''': 5 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes on foot from [[:en:Kyushu Railway Company|Kyushu Railway Company]]'s [[:en:Takajō Station|Takajō Station]] on the [[:en:Nippō Main Line|Nippō Main Line]].[http://www.oita-gokoku.jp/access/index.html Access] Ōita Prefecture Gokoku Shrine * '''By Bus''': 17 minutes on foot from Jōtō Middle School bus stop, accessible from [[:en:Ōita Station|Ōita Station]]. * '''By Car''': 20 minutes from [[Ōita-Mera Interchange]] on the [[:en:Ōita Expressway|Ōita Expressway]] or [[:en:Higashi Kyushu Expressway|Higashi
